endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: FUTURE-AI recommends that AI developers engage with healthcare professionals, domain experts, representative citizens, and/or ethicists early in the process to form interdisciplinary AI development teams and investigate in-depth the application specific sources of bias, which might include domain specific attributes (eg, breast density for AI applications in breast cancer).

endorsements.title: Health Equity Across the AI Lifecycle (HEAAL) framework
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership; PLOS Digital Health (PMID 38723025, doi:10.1371/journal.pdig.0000390)
endorsements.quote: Each procedure not only contains sub-procedures with detailed steps but also identifies relevant active stakeholders and data sources.

endorsements.title: Early Online
endorsements.issuer: South African medical journal = Suid-Afrikaanse tydskrif vir geneeskunde
endorsements.quote: In this context, the SAMA Task Team’s recommendation to embed ubuntu within accountability frameworks must be understood as a practical directive rather than a symbolic gesture: it requires genuine co‑creation with communities, transparent channels for reporting and responding to harm, and solidarity‑oriented deployment of AI tools so that innovations do not privilege urban, advantaged patients while marginalising rural or underserved populations.

commentary.bottom_line: No study in this map tests whether bias-reporting mechanisms for users and affected populations lead to more reports or less harm, or whether those procedures are fair in themselves. Two frameworks, FUTURE-AI and HEAAL, endorse stakeholder engagement and structured equity procedures, but that support rests on consensus rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. The support comes from one consensus guideline and one framework, and GRADE does not treat either type of source as evidence of effect. Certainty about whether reporting mechanisms surface bias, or whether the procedures change fairness, cannot be rated.

The recommendation asks that feedback procedures be checked for their own fairness. This matters because reporting channels may favor people with time, digital access, or English fluency. No study here measures who uses such channels or who is left out, so the risk of uneven reporting remains untested.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare bias-reporting channels (for example, clinician portals, patient hotlines, and community advisory input) on report volume, the demographics of reporters, how often reports are confirmed, and later changes in model performance across subgroups. The same studies should measure whether some groups report less often than others.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so there are no data on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. The populations that may face the most bias are also the ones whose ability to use reporting channels has not been measured.
